title: DR-Submodular Maximization with Stochastic Biased Gradients: Classical and Quantum Gradient Algorithms
claim: Quantum zero-order estimators match first-order convergence and consistently outperform classical zero-order ones across problems and constraint types.
layout: 3x3 grid of line plots, shared legend on top, row and column labels
description: A 3x3 grid of line plots shows function value against iteration count, from 0 to 100. A single legend bar across the top names three methods: classical first-order in blue, classical zero-order in orange, and quantum zero-order in green. Columns are constraint types: convex, down-closed convex, and convex with a largest element. Rows are problems: quadratic programming, finite sum, and coverage. In every panel the curves rise monotonically. Blue and green nearly overlap, with green slightly below or equal to blue. The jagged orange curve sits clearly lower. The eye goes first to the legend, then to the visible gap between the orange curve and the blue and green curves. Axes are minimal and have no titles.

abstract: In this work, we investigate DR-submodular maximization using stochastic biased gradients, which is a more realistic but challenging setting than stochastic unbiased gradients. We first generalize the Lyapunov framework to incorporate biased stochastic gradients, characterizing the adverse impacts of bias and noise. Leveraging this framework, we consider not only conventional constraints but also a novel constraint class: convex sets with a largest element, which naturally arises in applications such as resource allocations. For this constraint, we propose an $1/e$ approximation algorithm for non-monotone DR-submodular maximization, surpassing the hardness result $1/4$ for general convex constraints. As a direct application of stochastic biased gradients, we consider zero-order DR-submodular maximization and introduce both classical and quantum gradient estimation algorithms. In each constraint we consider, while retaining the same approximation ratio, the iteration complexity of our classical zero-order algorithms is $O(\epsilon^{-3})$, matching that of stochastic unbiased gradients; our quantum zero-order algorithms reach $O(\epsilon^{-1})$ iteration complexity, on par with classical first-order algorithms, demonstrating quantum acceleration and validated in numerical experiments.
